headline: 15 inches of rain in a day. South Florida shut its schools.
summary: A slow-moving storm dropped 15.3 inches of rain on parts of Broward County in the 24 hours to Wednesday. Hollywood declared an emergency, stretches of I-95 and the Turnpike closed, and a synagogue roof fell in. No injuries were reported. Schools in Broward and Miami-Dade close Thursday, and up to 12 more inches could fall by Friday.
cover_answer: It is. El Niño is steering storms south anyway.
table_question: Your car's wake pushes water into a house. Is that your fault?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: In Florida it rained so hard that cars got stuck in water on the big roads. Fifteen inches fell in one day, more than a school ruler standing on end. Nobody was hurt, and kids there get Thursday off school. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: A ruler on end is rain they can see. The rest is for us.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script turns 15 inches of rain into a school ruler standing on end. Cantor found the picture is what scares this age, so the stuck cars come with 'nobody was hurt' in the next breath. Expect 'could that happen here?' It can rain hard anywhere. This one is over Florida.

8-12.script: Florida is in its dry season, but a slow storm sat over Broward County and dropped 15.3 inches of rain in a day. Water covered roads, stalled cars on the highway, and a synagogue roof fell in. Like a bathtub with the tap running faster than the drain. Schools there are shut Thursday.
8-12.why: Rain faster than the drain is a chain they can check at home.
8-12.why_long: At nine a child is working out cause and effect, so the script runs the chain: a storm parks over one county, 15.3 inches fall, roads turn to water, a roof gives way, schools close. The bathtub is a mechanism they can test tonight. Expect 'why did the roof fall?' The report says heavy rain caused it and no more. Stop where it stops.

13-17.script: Why is it pouring in Florida's dry season? A Weather Service meteorologist says El Niño, a natural warming cycle, is steering storms south this year. Second: Fort Lauderdale's record for the day was 1.8 inches, set in 1959. Wednesday brought 5.72. Which one should a city build for?
13-17.why: Two things at once: a natural cycle, and a record tripled.
13-17.why_long: A thirteen-year-old can hold two true things: the meteorologist blames El Niño, a natural cycle, and a 1959 record was tripled in one morning. The script gives them both, then a question with no clean answer: which number a city should build for. Expect 'is this climate change?' The report doesn't say. Don't put in what it left out.

5-7.q: Could it rain that much here?
5-7.a: That storm is sitting over Florida. Heavy rain can happen anywhere, and grown-ups know what to do: stay off the roads until it drains.

8-12.a: No injuries were reported. The roof fell at Temple Sinai in Hollywood.
The report says heavy rain caused it, and nothing more. That's all we know.

13-17.a: It is. El Niño, a natural cycle, is steering storms south, the NWS says.
The report blames El Niño. It doesn't mention climate change. Stop there.
